title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

summary.text: The investigation plans spherical diffusion flame tests of C2H4 and CH4 flames in drop towers and aboard the International Space Station to obtain soot-inception and extinction limits.

geometry.text: Normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames.

pressure.text: Pressure is listed as a varied parameter; no values are given.

flow.text: Flow rate is listed as a varied parameter; no values are given.

gravity.text: Tests are planned in drop towers and aboard the International Space Station.

measurements.text: Cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.

hardware.text: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) and Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).

claims.text: The investigation aims to obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2), and pressure for C2H4 and CH4 flames.
The investigation aims to obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of N2, and pressure for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 flames.
The investigation hypothesizes that microgravity spherical diffusion flames extinguish when the peak temperature first decreases below 1130 K.
The investigation hypothesizes that steady-state spherical diffusion flames are possible.

limitations.text: The stated research impact concerns terrestrial combustors, not spacecraft fire safety.
Only PSI metadata was examined; no document text was processed.

modeling_resources.description: Experimental tables for normal and inverse flame runs, relevant to the planned flame measurements.

evidence.excerpt: Obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2), and pressure for C2H4 and CH4 flames.
Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of N2, and pressure for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 flames.
Microgravity spherical diffusion flames extinguish when the peak temperature first decreases below 1130 K.
Steady-state spherical diffusion flames are possible.
Perform spherical diffusion flame tests in drop towers and aboard the International Space Station.
Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.
Consider a broad range of reactant dilutions, flow rates and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions.
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME), Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)
improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors
